profile.summary: HyInv does inverse folding: given a protein backbone it proposes amino-acid sequences that should fold into it. The input is the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of a structure read from a PDB file; the output is a set of sequences, written as FASTA. It is a small graph network of 1,957,573 parameters that was trained first on natural and predicted structures and then by reinforcement learning against a structure predictor, and it ships as an installable Python package with its weights.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Usage, Layout; technical report Sections 2 and 2.1

summary_quotes.text: HyInv is a 1.96-million-parameter graph neural network for protein inverse folding
sees only the N, Cα, C and O backbone atoms, and runs on both CPU and GPU
pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyInv follows the message-passing encoder and decoder design of ProteinMPNN. Each residue is joined to its 48 nearest neighbours and the edges carry distance features that do not change with rotation or translation. The encoder has 4 layers of width 128 and runs once for a backbone; the decoder has 3 layers of the same width and predicts amino-acid distributions at the masked positions from the backbone and the residues already visible. Training had two stages: supervision that maximised the likelihood of the native sequence under a random residue order, then reinforcement learning whose reward was mostly the scTM between the predicted structure of a candidate sequence and the input backbone. At inference the model needs no protein language model, no structure predictor and no alignment.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3; README.md opening paragraph

quotes.text: HyInv follows the message-passing encoder–decoder of ProteinMPNN

Each residue is connected to its 48 nearest neighbors, and edges carry rotation- and translation-invariant distance features. The encoder has 4 layers of width 128 and runs once per backbone; the decoder has 3 layers of the same width.
At inference the model needs neither a protein language model, a structure predictor nor an alignment.
The decoder takes a partially masked sequence as input and predicts amino acid distributions at masked positions, conditioned on the backbone and the observed sequence context.
to maximize the likelihood of the native sequence under a random residue order
The RL stage rewards sequences whose predicted structure matches the input backbone.
It follows the message-passing design of ProteinMPNN with a 4-layer encoder and a 3-layer decoder

sections.title: Sampling: draft and rewrite
sections.body: Sequences are not drawn in one pass. The positions are split at random into 8 fixed groups. A draft phase samples one group per round at temperature 0.6 starting from a fully masked sequence, and a rewrite phase then masks one group per round, keeps every other position visible, and resamples that group at temperature 0.34. Generating a design costs one encoder pass and 16 decoder passes. The authors report that separating the two temperatures gives a higher scTM at the same sequence diversity than sampling at a single temperature, by 0.0078 on CATH4.3 test and 0.0131 on RecentPDB, measured on an earlier checkpoint of the same run.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.1 and 3.2; README.md opening paragraph

quotes.text: The sampler encodes the backbone once and splits the positions at random into R = 8 fixed groups

In the rewrite, round r masks the non-fixed positions in Gr , keeps all other positions unmasked, and resamples that group. Generation requires one forward pass through the encoder and 16 forward passes through the decoder
At equal diversity this gives a higher scTM than plain sampling at one temperature (Figure 1c): +0.0078 on CATH4.3 test and +0.0131 on RecentPDB, measured on an earlier checkpoint of the same run
deployment samples in 16 rounds — encode once, 8 rounds of blind drafting (temperature 0.6), then 8 rounds of rewriting by fixed groups (temperature 0.34)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: the reinforcement-learning version, which the technical report identifies as update 640 with draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, the setting used for every result in the report. The supervised checkpoint that preceded it is described but not released. A result should name the setting as well as the checkpoint, because the package offers three numerical paths. The default reference path is FP32 and reproduces its own output for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version; the exact path is accelerated FP32 and almost always returns the same sequences; the bf16 path is a different arithmetic and does not return the same sequences for the same seed. Batch size is part of the seed, because batch k uses seed plus k, and the CPU and GPU random streams differ.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.2 and 5.1, Table 1; README.md Notes and Accelerated inference

quotes.text: The HyInv default is the final checkpoint (update 640) with Td = 0.6 and Tr = 0.34, fixed on the development panel and used for every result in this report.
The released weights are the structure-reward reinforcement-learning version

Reproducibility: outputs are identical for the same `seed`, batch size (default 64, automatically tightened by length), device type and PyTorch version; each batch has its own random stream (batch k uses `seed+k`), so changing the batch size changes the result. The CPU and GPU random streams differ, so their sequences are not identical.
`bf16`: BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and tanh GELU, the fastest setting. This is a numerically-different path: sequences with the same seed are not identical to `off`

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Message-passing encoder and decoder in the style of ProteinMPNN: a 48-nearest-neighbour residue graph, an encoder of 4 layers at width 128 run once per backbone, and a decoder of 3 layers at the same width that reads a partly masked sequence.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: The N, C-alpha, C and O coordinates of the residues of a backbone, read from the ATOM records of the first model in a PDB file. One or more chains may be given; mmCIF has to be converted first. Positions can be pinned to their native residue.

quotes.text: The input is the N, Cα, C and O coordinates of L residues.
Input: ATOM records of the first model in the PDB file (MSE is treated as MET); each residue takes one slot, and residues with missing backbone atoms keep their slot and are designed
Convert mmCIF to PDB first.
Fixed positions are given by PDB residue number; they are visible as the native residue from the first round on and are kept unchanged in the output.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Sampled amino-acid sequences over the 20 standard residues, written to a FASTA file by the command line or returned as a list of strings by the Python API. Chains are separated by a slash in the output.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Supervised stage: 627,945 sequences with structures, 76,787 experimental and 551,158 predicted, for 85,000 updates. Reinforcement-learning stage: a pool of 50,000 backbones filtered against the benchmark panels with a same-source homology mask, with 32 candidates sampled for each of 256 backbones per update.

The 50,000 training backbones were filtered against the benchmark panels with a same-source homology mask.
Each update samples 32 candidates for each of 256 backbones from the policy and scores them with ESMFold2.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: Not reported as a date. The report describes the training sets by size, provenance and quality rules and says the benchmark panels were screened for homology to PDB and CATH entries before 2025, but it does not date the structures used for training, and it states that zero sequence overlap between training data and the evaluation panels is not claimed. The technical report itself is dated 2026-10-14.
facts.source_locator: technical report: Appendix on data and pool; Benchmarks

quotes.text: We do not claim zero sequence overlap between the training data and the evaluation panels.

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: Not stated as a maximum. No limit on backbone length is given. The reinforcement-learning pool had mean length 254 and range 48 to 512, and the RecentPDB panel ran from 42 to 978 residues with no length truncation. For memory, the report measures a peak of 811 MiB for 128 candidates at 402 residues with a batch of 32 on the bf16 path, against 4,323 MiB for the reference sampler, and notes that captured CUDA graphs hold GPU memory per backbone length and batch size.

strengths.text: Small and cheap to run. The model has under two million parameters and runs on CPU as well as GPU, and the only required dependencies are PyTorch, safetensors and numpy.
strengths.source_locator: README.md opening paragraph and Installation; pyproject.toml dependencies

quotes.text: sees only the N, Cα, C and O backbone atoms, and runs on both CPU and GPU
Python 3.10+ and PyTorch; the only other dependencies are `safetensors` and `numpy`.
dependencies = ["torch>=2.4", "safetensors>=0.4", "numpy"]

strengths.text: Fast enough for library screening on one GPU: the authors measure 128 designs for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on an NVIDIA H20 with the bf16 path, and 10,000 designs for a 250-residue backbone in 2.11 s.

quotes.text: HyInv designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on one NVIDIA H20, 52.1× faster than the reference implementation of the sampler
A library of 10,000 sequences for one backbone takes 2.11 s (4,740 sequences per second).

strengths.text: Needs nothing beyond the backbone at inference: no alignment, no protein language model and no structure predictor, and positions can be pinned so that a catalytic site or pocket is kept.
strengths.source_locator: Technical report Section 2.1 and Section 6; README.md Usage and Notes

quotes.text: At inference the model needs neither a protein language model, a structure predictor nor an alignment.
The same HyInv default setting serves four single-chain design tasks without task-specific tuning.
python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --chain A --fixed 12-20,45 --n 16   # keep residues 12-20 and 45

strengths.text: The developers report that on their five panels, with one panel scored by three structure predictors, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity. This is the authors' own evaluation.

quotes.text: Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset–predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity
HyInv has the highest scTM in all seven panel–predictor columns, and its average is 0.875, against 0.867 for ProteinZero V2 (ESM2) and 0.863 for ProteinMPNN.

limitations.text: Single chains only in intent. The authors state that HyInv targets single-chain backbones and name multi-chain interfaces and membrane environments as future work, although the command line accepts several chains.

quotes.text: HyInv targets single-chain backbones; designing for multi-chain interfaces and membrane environments is a natural next step.
For multi-chain structures pass `--chain AB`, or omit `--chain` to read all chains

limitations.text: The fast bf16 path does not reproduce the reference sequences, so a result must say which path produced it. The exact path reproduces them almost always: in a check of about 8,000 sequences one differed at one position.
limitations.source_locator: README.md Accelerated inference; technical report Section 4 and Table 1

quotes.text: This is a numerically-different path: sequences with the same seed are not identical to `off`
across about 8,000 independently checked sequences of varying length (including missing atoms, two chains and fixed positions), only one differed at one position
The exact FP32 path returns the same sequences as the reference sampler; the BF16 path (HyInv) changes the arithmetic slightly

limitations.text: The accelerated kernels were verified on one GPU only. The authors say they were verified with triton 3.3.1 on an H20 and should compile on other architectures but have not been checked there.

quotes.text: Verified on a Hopper-class GPU (H20, sm_90); the kernels should compile on other architectures but have not been verified.
verified with triton 3.3.1 on an H20

limitations.text: Reproducing a design set needs more than the seed. Changing the batch size changes the output, because batch k uses seed plus k, and the CPU and GPU random streams differ.

run_guide.summary: Install the hyinv package from a checkout of the repository and design sequences for one PDB backbone.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or newer, as pyproject.toml requires, with PyTorch 2.4 or newer.
safetensors and numpy; triton 3.3 or newer only for the accelerated paths, which need a CUDA build of PyTorch.
A PDB file of the backbone. mmCIF has to be converted to PDB first.
No GPU is needed: the sources say the model runs on both CPU and GPU.
MIT licence, so no registration and no licence acceptance step.

steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results.git
cd Hyra-results
git checkout --detach b24e7f5543f08069fe190e98c5c05b62ca28a074
cd AI4Science/hyinv
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command. The clone, checkout and cd lines are added here to get the package directory at the commit this page was written from. The weights ship in the repository, so there is nothing else to download.

quotes.text: `weights/`: `model.safetensors` (FP32, 7.8 MB) and `config.json`

steps.shell:
pip install -e .
# optional, CUDA GPUs only:
# pip install -e '.[fast]'
steps.explanation: Installs the package in place. The second line, left commented out, adds triton for the accelerated paths and is only useful with a CUDA build of PyTorch.

quotes.text: pip install -e .
pip install -e '.[fast]'   # optional: accelerated inference on CUDA GPUs
fast = ["triton>=3.3"]

steps.title: Design sequences for a backbone
steps.explanation: The README's own example. It reads all chains of structure.pdb, samples 128 sequences with the default reference path on the default device, and writes them to designs.fasta. Replace structure.pdb with your own file.

quotes.text: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --n 128 --seed 0 --out designs.fasta

steps.title: Keep chosen residues, or use the Python API
steps.shell:
python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --chain A --fixed 12-20,45 --n 16

python - <<'PY'
from hyinv import HyInv, read_pdb, design

model = HyInv.from_pretrained(device="cuda")          # reads the bundled weights/ by default
structure = read_pdb("structure.pdb", chains="A")
sequences = design(model, structure, n=8, seed=0, fixed="12-20,45")   # list[str]
PY
steps.explanation: The first line keeps residues 12 to 20 and 45 of chain A at their native identity. The Python block is the README's API example, wrapped in a shell heredoc; it asks for the cuda device, so pass device="cpu" on a machine without a GPU.

quotes.text: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --chain A --fixed 12-20,45 --n 16   # keep residues 12-20 and 45
model = HyInv.from_pretrained(device="cuda")          # reads the bundled weights/ by default

From the Python API, a list of sequence strings.
Fixed positions appear unchanged in the output.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The default path is the FP32 reference implementation. Adding --fast exact or --fast bf16 needs a CUDA GPU and triton, and bf16 does not return the same sequences as the default.
The sources give no memory requirement, and the only GPU named anywhere is the NVIDIA H20 used for the authors' timings.
The example file name structure.pdb is the README's placeholder, not a file in the repository.
